title: Zapier CEO: 80% of agent tasks should be deterministic code
dek: Wade Foster says 80% of what customers do with agents should really be old-fashioned deterministic code; no code is over, and the new no code is code.
why: A first-hand post-mortem on Zapier betting on MCP, agents, SDKs and guardrails at once, including Automation Bench and how AI transformation is done internally.
who: Founders building agent or automation products, engineering leads weighing model price-performance, and managers pushing AI adoption inside their companies.
skip: The sponsor read and the closing recommendations can be skipped; the rest is evenly dense.

points.h: Knowledge work is moving into people's everyday tools
points.body: Foster walks through his biggest shift in thinking over the past 18 months: most people have already picked a daily AI tool — maybe Cursor, Claude Code or ChatGPT — and that is where the work happens. So getting context and data into that daily tool (an MCP server like Zapier MCP, for instance) is where knowledge work is heading. He splits the market in two: one camp wants to keep people on its own platform building agents, the other, like Salesforce, goes headless and lets you take it wherever you want. He is explicit that the latter is the winning strategy, because that is what tool consumers want and where the growth is.

points.h: The strongest model gets only 40% of automation tasks right
points.body: Zapier's Automation Bench tests models on roughly 600 real knowledge-work tasks, for example ‘just signed the Meridian Core platform contract, mark it as won per the routing policy and hand it to the right team, confirm the account from the account hierarchy table, convert currency if needed, and check whether there is an open support escalation’. Foster says the newest strongest model lands at about 40% accuracy, the highest so far, but costs far more than Gemini 3.7, which creates a curve of ‘how much are you willing to pay for incremental performance’. He stresses the benchmark is nowhere near saturated, and what Zapier wants to prove is that putting Zapier next to an agent produces better output than the model alone.

points.h: 80% of agent tasks should use deterministic code
points.body: Foster's core judgment: the vast majority of what customers do with agentic products — his number is 80% — should really use old-fashioned deterministic code. The approach is to have the agent first decide which steps to write as code (cheaper, more reliable), and only call AI or build an agent where reasoning is genuinely needed. He concedes models will keep getting better, but finds it hard to imagine a world where deterministic code is no longer more reliable and cheaper. He also keeps the visual layer: people still need to see what the workflow looks like, to verify ‘is this what I want it to do’, and to use it as documentation.

points.h: The real rival is the product director who leaves in two years
points.body: Asked what kind of competitor he worries about most, Foster brings up what PG said back at YC: the question then was not ‘what if Anthropic or OpenAI does this’ but ‘what if Google does this’, and what PG wanted to instil was that you rarely fight Google directly — you face a mid-level product director who wants a promotion and will be gone in two years. He says OpenAI and Anthropic are now big companies and will be strongest on models, but they cannot do everything. On the other side, ordinary AI users have actually done nothing, maybe only used ChatGPT or Gemini, so most companies are not competing with each other but with whether people even know what to do with these tools.

points.h: Let AI watch you work and find automation opportunities for you
points.body: Foster thinks the hardest part has always been recommendations: what should you do with this thing. This year he started running a workflow where AI looks at his own daily activity in Gmail, Slack, the browser and chat, then tells him ‘you should do this differently’. Most Zapier employees plug their tools into Zapier MCP, run an automation once a week, collect a week of work signals, and get ‘you did this and this, here is a tool I suggest you build’. He says half the battle is just getting you to react to a suggestion — the idea does not need to be perfect, 50% good is enough to start brainstorming. He confirms this will very likely be productised.

points.h: The bottleneck in AI transformation shifted from tech to people
points.body: Foster says phase one was company-wide AI fluency: within a year nearly 100% of employees used AI daily, and technical adoption was not the bottleneck. After that the question became how to turn individual success into company-level production-grade workflows, so the challenge looks more and more like a people problem — rewriting job descriptions, rethinking compensation, reorganising teams, retraining people from teams you do not need into teams you do. Brandon, the people officer at the time, was good at this and the team was on the frontier, so he was asked to help the whole company. Foster stresses this is not a claim that ‘the people officer must own AI’: a CMO or CPO could do it too; the point is to see where your bottleneck is and then find the right person.

points.h: Some people burn $30,000 of tokens a month
points.body: Foster says a few individual engineers spend $30,000 a month on tokens, which is an outlier. Zapier currently sets no per-person budget, but has built tools so people can see their own spend and see the cost difference between a strong model and a cheap model on different workflows. When he sees someone spending especially much, his first reaction is to talk: ‘what are you doing, I'm curious’. It turns out some are doing extremely high-output work, while others are using Fable or Astro where it is not needed. He expects token budgets will eventually become a real thing, and that part of AI fluency is some people getting a higher budget because they use it better.

points.h: Using AI is not the problem, low quality is
points.body: Foster says he is not against employees using AI to write communications; the real problem is low-quality communication: people with poor judgment can produce a huge volume of low-quality content extremely fast and drown the reader. A few of his rules: you are responsible for what you send, and the author should spend more time than the reader; you should understand what you sent and not be unable to answer follow-up questions; make requests explicit — do you want a decision, feedback, or is this marked as a draft; verify details, because AI hallucinates and may also pull up a project from three months ago as relevant material, and summaries of summaries passed down the chain turn into misinformation. He also calls out the AI voice — ‘not this, but that’, em dashes, honest truth, load-bearing point.
